1001.quote_or_event: “Gathering in and hoarding what they can, the faithless cynics die, O Nanak, but the wealth of Maya does not go with them in the end.”
1001.explanation: In a salok of Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan describes those who spend their lives piling up wealth, die, and find that none of it goes with them.
1001.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder fills his house and dies with nothing done through his wealth; Guru Arjan pictures the same person dying in the middle of his gathering.
1001.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 257, Raag Gauri, Bavan Akhri (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1001._accuracy_note: Close fit on hoarding until death; Gurbani adds that the hoarder is spiritually dead (saakat, cut off from God), which goes further than the Kural's practical verdict.

1002.quote_or_event: “People gather and hoard their possessions, and give nothing to anyone else - the poor fools think that everything is theirs.”
1002.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the hoarder gives nothing away because he is blind: he thinks everything he holds belongs to him.
1002.tie_back: The Kural blames the delusion that wealth is everything for the miser's refusal to give; Guru Nanak likewise ties the refusal to give to a blind belief that it is all his own.
1002.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1002._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on delusion and not giving; the Kural's further point, that this delusion leads to a debased birth, is only implied here.

1003.quote_or_event: “Earning a thousand, he runs after a hundred thousand. Satisfaction is not obtained by chasing after Maya.”
1003.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the restless accumulator who earns a thousand and at once runs after a hundred thousand, never satisfied.
1003.tie_back: The Kural condemns people greedy only for piling up wealth; Guru Arjan pictures that endless piling up and shows that it never brings contentment.
1003.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278-279, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1003._accuracy_note: Strong on greed for accumulation; the Kural's contrast with a good name (isai) and its image of being a burden to the earth are not in this passage.

1004.quote_or_event: “The kings die, gathering and hoarding their money, burying great quantities of gold.”
1004.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, points to kings who spent their lives hoarding and burying gold, and died with it still in the ground.
1004.tie_back: The Kural asks what legacy a man whom no one loves can leave; Kabir's buried gold is the hoarder's only legacy, of use to no one.
1004.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 654, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1004._accuracy_note: Next-best match: Kabir speaks of hoarding and death but not of being unloved by others, which is the Kural's central point.

1005.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
1005.explanation: Guru Nanak names the right use of earnings: live on what you have earned by honest work and give part of it to others. This salok is the scriptural root of kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing).
1005.tie_back: The Kural names enjoying and giving as the two uses of wealth, without which crores are worth nothing; Guru Nanak names the same two, eating what one earns and giving some away.
1005.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1005._accuracy_note: Strong fit on enjoying and giving; Guru Nanak also stresses that the wealth must be earned by one's own labour, which the Kural does not raise here.

1006.quote_or_event: “He hoards gold and silver, but this wealth is false and poisonous, nothing more than ashes.”
1006.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak says that gold and silver piled up for their own sake are false, poisonous and as worthless as ashes.
1006.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who neither enjoys nor gives a disease to his own great wealth; Guru Nanak calls such hoarded wealth poison and ash.
1006.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 937, Raag Ramkali, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1006._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it fits the reading in which the wealth itself becomes harmful, but says nothing of giving to the worthy.

1007.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the young Nanak was given money by his father Mehta Kalu to make a profitable bargain (sacha sauda), but on the way he met a group of hungry holy men and spent all of it on food for them, calling this the true bargain.
1007.explanation: The story is remembered as the first act of the Sikh duty to share with the needy, later embodied in the langar.
1007.tie_back: The Kural says wealth never given to the destitute is wasted like beauty that ages alone; the young Nanak's true bargain is the opposite, money spent at once on those who had nothing.
1007.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak
1007._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on giving to the destitute, but the story is hagiography from the Janamsakhis rather than a historical record, and the Kural's simile of the woman ageing alone has no Sikh parallel.

1008.quote_or_event: “The Simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
1008.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak uses the tall silk-cotton tree as an image of imposing greatness that offers nothing to those who come to it in hope.
1008.tie_back: The Kural compares the unloved man's wealth to a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town; Guru Nanak's towering tree likewise stands in full view and sends everyone away empty.
1008.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1008._accuracy_note: Very close image of a conspicuous but useless tree; Guru Nanak turns it toward humility and sweetness rather than hoarded wealth specifically.

1009.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
1009.explanation: Reflecting on the wealth of rulers ruined in Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says that such riches are never amassed without wrongdoing and are left behind at death.
1009.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gathered by abandoning love and virtue will be taken by others; Guru Nanak says it is gathered through sin and stays behind when its owner dies.
1009.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Ashtpadi (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1009._accuracy_note: Strong fit on wealth gained without regard for virtue and left behind; the Kural's detail of self-denial in the getting is not in the verse.

1010.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
1010.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks of a treasure that grows the more it is shared and spent together. In context the treasure is the Lord's Name inherited from the Guru.
1010.tie_back: The Kural says the brief poverty of generous men is like a cloud spent by its rain that soon fills again; Guru Arjan speaks of a store that never runs out however much is given away.
1010.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1010._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the idea that giving does not exhaust the giver is shared, but Guru Arjan's treasure is spiritual (the Naam), not the material wealth of the Kural's generous rich man.
